items.title: Gemini 4 Argon (In-depth benchmark analysis): Did Google make a big comeback?
items.summary:
In this video, I'll be analyzing Google’s new Gemini 4 Argon model, including its performance across business workflows, coding, spreadsheets, long-context reasoning, cybersecurity, hallucination tests, and independent benchmarks. I’ll also break down its introductory pricing, future standard rates, limited availability, and whether it offers enough value to compete with Claude, GPT-6 Astra, and GPT-6.1 Sol.

--
Key Takeaways:

🚀 Gemini 4 Argon leads several independent benchmarks for professional workflows, spreadsheets, and economic-value tasks.
📊 Argon takes the top spot on the Vals Index and performs strongly on Zapier’s AutomationBench.
💻 Coding performance is mixed, with excellent DeepSWE results but weaker scores on FrontierSWE and Terminal-Bench.
🧠 Argon appears more willing to admit uncertainty, achieving a notably low hallucination rate on AA-Omniscience.
📚 Its long-context capabilities look promising, with support for up to one million output tokens and strong GraphWalks res

items.transcript: [music] >> Hi. Welcome to another video. So, Google has announced Gemini 4 Argon, and there are some pretty interesting results here. It leads an independent benchmark for business workflows, takes the top spot on the Valves index, and looks much better at admitting when it doesn't know something. But, the coding results are mixed, and the pricing has a catch that changes the value comparison quite a bit. I've gone through Google's announcement, evaluation footnotes, and results from artificial analysis, Valves, Zapier, Surge, Arena, and the people behind CWE bench. This is an analysis of their published testing. I haven't run my own hands-on tests with Argon yet. My initial take is that this looks like a serious option for professional work with enough weaknesses that I wouldn't move my entire coding workflow over just because of the launch charts. So, let's get right into it. And there's a reason I'm cautious with Google. I've been disappointed by some of the previous Gemini releases, especially when the impressive reasoning scores didn't match what I wanted from a coding agent. With Gemini 3.1 Pro, my one-shot KingBench result was actually very good at 96% but my agent testing had repeated planning problems using the tools, and basic coding mistakes. On one go task, it duplicated a method and caused a compiler error. That's the kind of thing a headline reasoning score doesn't tell you. Those were particular runs in a particular setup, but they were enough to make me question its usefulness for my workflow. Then Gemini 3.5 Flash disappointed me on value. Its standard prices were one par at $50 for input and nine tars for output per million tokens, compared with 50 cents and $3 for Gemini 3 Flash. That's three times the token price. For something carrying the Flash name, I wanted a much stronger reason to pay that difference. And there was the wait for Gemini 3.5 Pro at I/O in May. Google said it expected to roll it out the following month. By its July 22 earnings call, it was still in testing. Now we're looking at another flagship announcement with limited initial access. I understand taking more time to get a model ready, but the earlier timeline gives me a reason to wait for actual availability before getting too excited. So, Argon has some confidence to earn back. That makes the independent results especially useful here. I want to give Google credit where it has improved while checking whether it has fixed the things that made those earlier releases frustrating. First, access. The initial rollout is through Google's Fairwind program for selected cybersecurity partners. Google says wider access will start with paid API customers and Google AI Ultra subscribers, but the announcement doesn't give a public release date. So, buying a subscription today shouldn't be treated as a guarantee that you can immediately use Argon. Now, let's start with the independent results because these help put the announcement in context. On Artificial Analysis, Argon had high reasoning scores, 53 on the Intelligence Index. That's the same rounded score as GPT-6 Astra at max reasoning and one point above GPT-6.1 Sonnet at max. Opus 5.5 scores 58 and Sonnet 5.5 scores 56, both at max with default fallback routing for refusals. So, Google is competitive here, although Anthropic is still ahead on this particular overall measure. Also, these are index points. A score of 53 doesn't mean it completes 53% of your work. And a one-point lead doesn't mean you're going to notice an improvement on every task. The Valse Index gives Argon a stronger result. It scores 68.9% ahead of Sonnet 5.5 at about 67% and Opus 5.5 at about 67%. Valse combines finance, coding, legal, and tax benchmarks with weights based on those sectors' shares of the US economy. One detail I like here is that Valse already uses Argon's higher standard token prices in its cost calculation. Even then, it reports about $15.68 per test versus 21.34 for Sonnet and $32.14 for Opus. So, there's a real value argument within this suite. But, finance accounts for a little over half of that index's weighting. If most of your day is fixing code, that overall ranking might not reflect your priorities. I'd look at the coding components before deciding which model to use. Zapier's automation bench is another strong result. Argon at high reasoning gets 51.29% compared with 44.75% for Sonnet 5.5 at max with its default fallback routing. This benchmark checks whether an agent actually completes workflows across simulated business apps. That means checking the records and other changes it leaves behind. The model saying that it completed the task doesn't earn it a pass. Every required check has to succeed, which I think is a useful way to evaluate automation. Argon is ahead here, and that's good to see. But, roughly half the tasks still don't pass every check. For me, that supports using it to assist with these workflows while checking the results. It doesn't establish that you can leave it to run a business without supervision. There's another independent win on Surge's GDP.xlsx spreadsheet benchmark. Argon scores 38.3% compared with 30.3% for Opus 5.5 and 29.1% for Sonnet 5.5. This is a rubric-based score, so don't read it as the percentage of spreadsheets it completed perfectly. Taken together, those results make the professional work pitch look pretty credible. I'd be interested in testing it on a messy workbook where it has to follow references across sheets and explain how it arrived at the answer. That's the sort of task where checking a few easy cells isn't enough. Anyway, now let's come to coding because this is where the picture gets more complicated. Google reports 77.9% on Deep Way U version 1.1 ahead of Opus 5.5 at 74.2% and Astra at 74.1% in its comparison. That's a strong result. But, on Frontier's way version 2, Argon gets 55% while Astra gets 65.5% and Opus gets 62.3% and on Google's Terminal Bench 4 comparison, Argon is at 57.4% versus 66.4% for Opus. So, even within Google's own table, the answer changes depending on which software engineering test you look at. There's a methodology detail here, too. Google computed Argon's Deep Stew AU result with Mini Stew AU agent, while Astra's comes from the benchmark leaderboard and Claude's from system cards. These are separately published evaluations. I'd want a controlled comparison in the same agent setup before attributing every difference to the model. Vala independently puts Argon second on both its app building and code migration benchmarks behind Sonnet 5.5. That is encouraging, but the app building gap is less than half a percentage point, smaller than the reported standard errors. I wouldn't make a big deal out of who is first or second there. For coding, my reading is that Argon deserves testing on substantial tasks, especially migrations and app building. The results don't give me a reason to assume it will consistently beat your current agent on debugging, terminal work, and difficult repository changes. This is also why I wouldn't just count how many rows Google wins. A chart reading improvement and a repository fixing improvement aren't interchangeable when you're choosing something for your daily work. One more example is the legal result. Argon's 19.6% looks dominant against the models Google selected for its chart, but Vala's own Argon report lists it fifth for the Harvey legal evaluation. That doesn't erase the result. The launch comparison simply doesn't establish that it leads the whole field. Now, the hallucination result is probably the most interesting part of this release for me. Artificial Analysis reports a 15% hallucination rate on AA Omniscients, the lowest among the models scoring at least 45 on its intelligence index. Astra at max is at 51%. However, Argon's knowledge accuracy is 50% compared with Astra's 63%. Those numbers can sound contradictory until you check the definition. The hallucination metric looks at the responses that weren't correct and measures how often the model gave an incorrect answer instead of a partial answer or an admission that it didn't know. Correct answers aren't in that denominator. So, 15% doesn't mean 15% of everything Argon says is false. It also doesn't mean it has solved hallucinations. The useful result is that it is more willing to acknowledge gaps even though it answers fewer of these questions correctly than Astra. Personally, I like that trade-off for research. If a model can't support a claim, I'd like it to say so. A confident answer with a made-up API or reference can waste a lot of time, but I still want to check how that behavior carries over to browsing and coding where the model has tools available to verify things. Arena gives us a different kind of evidence. Its September 30th text leaderboard puts Argon high at number one with a score of 1525 and around 4,900 votes. The result is marked preliminary. That's encouraging for how people respond to its answers. It also helps explain why a model can look excellent in chat without topping every technical benchmark. Human preference, factual knowledge, and successfully changing a code base are separate things. I'd use the Arena result as another signal alongside the task-based tests. Now, Google also highlights a million token output limit. The output part matters. This gives a reasoning trajectory much more room to continue working. It isn't just a claim about how much material you can put into the prompt. Artificial Analysis says it tested a feature called long decode continuation, which pauses long responses and resumes them through follow-up calls, allowing reasoning to reach that limit without request timeouts. So, the practical question is whether that extra thinking produces a better result at a cost you're happy with. I don't need a model to write a million tokens for a small bug fix, for a difficult optimization problem. I'd be more willing to spend that time and money if it produces something I can verify. There's a separate long context result, too. Google's reported graph walks result covers context between 256,000 and 1 million tokens. Argon scores 84.2 on the F1 metric compared with Astra's 71.8. That's promising for following relationships across long inputs, although one graph benchmark can't establish how well it understands every large repository. And the video results need a footnote. Google reports 91.7% on LVBench, but its methodology uses one frame per second for Gemini and fixed frame caps for competitors because of their API limits. That can be a practical advantage for the Gemini setup, but it isn't an equal input test of visual reasoning. Cybersecurity has some similarly useful detail. On CWE Bench version 1, Argon ties Astra and Grok 4.7 at 68% under the programmatic single attempt measure. Under the separate judge panel measure, Argon gets 62% while Opus gets 67%. The benchmark also lists $63 per rollout for Argon and 79 cents for Opus. Those figures use different agent harnesses, and the Argon calculation uses a cached input price that differs from Google's introductory discount. So, I wouldn't turn that into a universal cost ratio. But it does show why the score, grading method, and spending all deserve a look before calling something the best security agent. Now, let's talk about the API pricing because this could change whether Argon makes sense for you. Google advertises $2 per million dollar input tokens and $10 per million output tokens with a 95% discount on cached input. The footnote says the prices become $4 and $20 after the introductory period. Google hasn't given an exact end date in the announcement. That is a doubling of the input and output rates. If you're budgeting for an application, I would calculate the cost at the standard rate and treat the launch price as a temporary benefit. Artificial analysis measures about 199 per intelligence index task at the promotional rate. It calculates $3.98 after the discount ends. Astra at max costs about $3.26 on that same evaluation, while GPT-6.1 Soul at max costs about $0.72. That changes the comparison quite a bit. Argon looks cheaper than Astra at launch, but more expensive after the promotion on this workload. Soul is much cheaper while scoring only one index point lower. Your own task mix could produce a different result, but you shouldn't choose based only on the price per million tokens. Artificial Analysis also reports around 62,000 output tokens per task for Argon, compared with around 27,000 for Astra. So, that lower unit price is doing a lot of work. The amount the model generates matters, too, and efficiency isn't the same across evaluations. Remember that Valves still puts Argon below Sonnet and Opus in cost per test using its standard price. That's why I want to measure the bill for the actual job, how much it costs to get a patch accepted or a work book checked, including any retries. I also wouldn't promise that Argon feels fast in an editor yet. Artificial Analysis doesn't publish an output speed measurement for it on the model page. Valves has task duration numbers, but those don't tell us how responsive the eventual public service will feel while you're working. So, how good is Gemini 4 Argon looking overall? I think the strongest case is professional work where it needs to follow information across documents and tools, plus tasks where admitting uncertainty is useful. There are several independent results supporting that case, so I wouldn't dismiss this as a model that only looks good in Google's own charts. For coding, I'm more cautious. It has strong results in some areas and clear losses in others. I try it on a migration or a difficult task that my usual model struggled with, then compare the finished result and the total cost. I wouldn't assume a new model name means I should rebuild my workflow around it. The things I want to test when access opens are fairly practical. Can it finish changes without quietly dropping requirements? Can it recover after a failed approach? And does giving it more time actually improve the patch enough to justify the extra tokens? At the introductory price, Argon looks worth trying. At the standard price, I would be more selective about which jobs I send to it. The evidence gives Google a credible contender here after the earlier disappointments. Consistent results in the tools we actually use would do the most to win back my confidence. The weak part is the bite. There is a round piece of bun sitting near the mouth with an awkward cutout underneath it, so it doesn't read as a clean bite taken from the burger. You can understand the intended scene, but the overlap between the mouth and the food could be much better. This is a static SVG, and that's fine because animation wasn't required. It gets 7 out of 10. Sui 2 gets eight, Groke 47 gets four, and both GPT6 soul and Opus 5.5 get 10. Now, let's come to the archery game. The requirement is four targets with faster completion moving the player up a leaderboard. At first, the presentation looks promising. It creates a landscape with mountains, a bright sun, grass, an archer, and a heads up display showing the timer, wind, targets, and arrows. There is a draw and release interaction and a dotted guide for the arrows trajectory. But when I start the game, the target stands appear across the range, while the actual target faces are piled up in the top left corner. So, the things you're supposed to aim at aren't displayed where the game checks for hits. The code confirms the problem. It draws the target circles around the canvas origin without first moving the drawing position to each target's location. There's also a separate error in the moving forth target. Its animation uses a starting height that was never defined. And the timer has a problem, too. After I fired an arrow, it stopped at 1.24 seconds while I was preparing the next shot. The timer pauses whenever you're aiming between shots, so it leaves out part of the time you're actually playing. That matters because this is supposed to be a time trial. A leaderboard based on that timer wouldn't measure how quickly you actually completed the round. And the broken fourth target prevents a normal four target finish. Anyway, so nice scenery, but major gameplay issues. This gets four out of 10. Sway 2 and Grock 4.7 gets seven, GPT6, Soul gets six, and Opus 5.5 gets nine. The sixth test is the math problem. We have 60 ordered pairs arranged across 20 possible x values and three possible y-v values with specific rules for how consecutive pairs can connect. We need to count the valid orderings starting on the top row and ending on the bottom row. The expected answer in the benchmark is 20,460 and m3.1 flash is recorded as correct with 10 out of 10. All five models in the comparison sheet get 10 on this one. So this is a full score result but it doesn't separate these models. Now the seventh test is much more ambitious. It asks the model to create a data set of panda facts, fine-tune a Gemma 2 billion parameter model and build a local web interface that produces a fact whenever the page refreshes. And there is substantial work here. The project contains 184 distinct facts expanded into 920 training examples and 184 validation examples. It uses a 4-bit Gemma 22B model with Laura adapters which are a smaller set of trainable weights added to the base model. There are actual saved model files and adapter weights. The training log reaches 600 iterations and the reported validation loss drops from 3.893 to 0.207. So this isn't just a page with a random sentence and a claim that training happened. The interface is called aopota. It has a warm paper colored background, large serif text for the fact, a category underneath, and another fact button. I opened the local app, clicked that button, and refreshed the page. It did produce different entries, but there are important limitations. The validation examples use the same facts as training with different prompts. So, that lower loss shows improvement on that narrow data set. It doesn't prove the model can reliably answer new Panda questions. Also, the app compares generated text with its own data set and can replace a close match with the stored wording. When it says verified, it means matched to that corpus. It doesn't mean an independent source checked the statement. And I actually saw why that distinction matters. One displayed entry said the panda's digestive system is built for bamboo rather than flesh. Smithsonian's National Zoo describes it as more similar to a carnivore's digestive system. And another entry in this project's own data set says essentially the same thing. So the corpus contains a contradiction. There is a lot to like about the local pipeline, but the data quality and reliability need work. This gets 7 out of 10, while the other four models in the sheet get 10. Finally, we have the 3D wristwatch. This needs to show the current time with smooth hands, included day and date, and track two time zones. The result is called Meridian GMT, and it is quite ambitious. It has a metal case, a strap wrapped around a display wrist, a crown, a dark dial, day and date windows, and a separate hand for the second time zone. There are controls for the dial color, strap, hand movement, lighting, and camera angle. The live clock works in the preview. I changed the second time zone from London to Tokyo, and the readout updated from 5 hours ahead of New York to 13 hours ahead. The hand animation also uses fractional seconds, which is what you want for smooth movement, but the face has a very obvious geometry problem. The hour markers are all bunched near the top, forming this strange star-shaped cluster instead of being spread around the dial. The code gives them the same starting position and rotates each marker locally rather than placing it around the center of the watch. The outer numbers also appear upside down. And clicking the dial camera preset brings us to a steep almost edge on view that makes the face harder to inspect when the button should help you see it. So the timekeeping and customization are there, but the actual watch face needs fixing. This gets 5 out of 10. SWE2 gets eight, Grock 4.7 gets six, and GPT6 Soul and Opus 5.5 both get 10. Now let's look at the final scores. M3.1 flash gets three for the elevator, eight for the contact lens case, nine for the folding table, seven for the Panda SVG, four for archery, 10 for math, seven for the local training task, and five for the watch. That adds up to 53 out of 80 or 66.25%. In the detailed comparison, Gro 4.7 gets 62 out of 80 or 77.5%. GPT6 Soul at medium gets 66 or 82.5%. Sweat 2 gets 67 or 83.75%. And Opus 5.5 at medium gets 75 which is 93.75%. The separate leaderboard graphic says 93.5 for opus but 75 out of 80 gives us 93.75. So I'm using the detailed sheet for that comparison. Looking at the full leaderboard M3.1 flash sits just above croc 4.5 at 65 and below Q3.8 flash next at 70. Above those GPT 5.6 Soul and Muse Spark 1.3 both have 71.25. 25. DSV4 flash has 72.5 and GLM 5.2 has 75. Muse Spark 1.2 and DSV4 Pro both have 76.25. Kimmy K3, Opus 5 and Grock 4.7 are tied at 77.5. GLM 5.3 Flash has 78.75 and Opus 4.8 has 80, Quen 3.8 max, Gemini 3.8 Flash and Deepseek V4.1 Flash all have 81.25. 25 GPT6 Soul and Fable 5 have 82.5 followed by SWE2 at 83.75 and the 3.8 MAX0902 entry at 86.25 at the top GPT6 Astra has 90, GLM 5.3 has 91.25, Fable 5.1 has 92.5 and then we have Opus 5.5 with the percentage discrepancy I just mentioned. Below M3.1 flash we have Muse Spark 1.1 at 60, GPT 5.6 Terra at 56.25, 25, Opus 4.7 at 50, Sonnet 5 at 48.75, GPT 5.6 Luna at 40, and GPT 5.5 at 35. The earlier Miniax M3 entry has 31.25, Gemini 3.5, Flash has 30. The separately labeled Deepseek V4 Pro entry has 24.8, and High3 has 20. Those are the labels and values shown in the supplied chart. In particular, it lists Deepseek V4 Pro and DS V4 Pro separately, so I wouldn't silently combine those entries without knowing the difference between the runs. So, the big improvement over Miniax M3 is clear in this benchmark, but M3.1 Flash still trails the stronger models overall, and its results vary a lot depending on the task. Personally, I like the folding table and the contact lens case gives us a useful starting point. The local training project also shows that it can put together several real components, including data preparation, training, inference, and a web interface. The problem is that some basic mistakes survive into the finished output. A button crashes before spawning anything. Target graphics are drawn in the wrong place. Watch markers all share the same position. These are issues that a quick browser check can reveal. So, if you're trying it for prototypes, inspect the result and test the main interaction before building on top of it. The score improvement is encouraging, but I would still want better consistency before trusting it with less supervision. And without verified pricing for this exact model or measured generation speed, I wouldn't declare it the best value just because it has flash in the name. Overall, it's pretty cool. items.summary:
In this video, I’ll explain Anthropic’s recommendations for getting better results from Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Code. We’ll cover clearer prompts, adaptive thinking, unfinished tasks, subagents, frontend design, testing, model switching, fast mode pricing, and practical ways to improve your AI coding workflow.

--
Key Takeaways:

🎯 Give Claude a clear definition of “finished” and specify the behaviors you expect it to implement and verify.
🧠 Remove generic instructions like “think carefully,” since Opus 5.5 uses adaptive thinking and configurable effort levels.
✅ Use Claude dot md instructions to encourage Claude Code to complete routine work and report genuine blockers.
📝 Maintain a tasks dot md file for long-running jobs so progress, completed checks, and blockers remain easy to inspect.
🤖 Use focused subagents for independent investigations, but verify their findings with code references or reproducible evidence.
🎨 Describe specific interface requirements instead of vaguely askin
